title: Workload-to-Hardware Fit & Scheduler Evaluation Manual
author: Priya Nair
content:
Overview
=======

This manual describes a repeatable process for characterizing production inference workloads, mapping them to appropriate accelerator classes, and evaluating scheduler/kernel policies to meet SLOs while minimizing cost. It consolidates profiling playbook steps, benchmark harness configuration, acceptance criteria for rollouts, common failure modes, and lightweight runbook actions for operational teams.

Goals
-----
- Produce a deterministic workload fingerprint (latency shape, token density, sequence distribution, KV-cache affinity).
- Map fingerprints to a small set of hardware classes (e.g., H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB, T4-16GB) with expected cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Evaluate scheduler knobs (batching, slotting, preemption, kernel hints) and quantify their impact on per-token cost, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU utilization.
- Provide a decision checklist for model-variant selection and fallback policies.

Scope and audience
------------------
This doc targets SREs, runtime engineers, and applied ML engineers responsible for: model onboarding, canary design, Dedicated capacity sizing, and private deployment sizing. It assumes familiarity with the runtime tracing tooling (trace-proxy, kernel-hint annotations) and the benchmarking harness in tools/perf-harness.

Key definitions
---------------
- Request shape: immutable properties of a request — prompt tokens, expected response token cap, streaming vs non-streaming.
- Sequence distribution: histogram of input+output lengths across a sample window.
- Affinity: the probability that successive requests share KV cache entries (session/conv affinity).
- Fidelity class: mapping of model/quantization/profile that yields a certain output quality and cost.

1) Workload fingerprinting (profiling playbook)
------------------------------------------------
Step-by-step (safe for production):
1. Identify a representative capture window (3–6 hours of typical traffic or per-release 24h). Prefer business-hours and a 24h weekend slice for consumer apps.
2. Shadow-capture requests using trace-proxy with disabled side-effects. Capture fields: timestamp, user/session id, model, route, seq_len_in, seq_len_out_cap, kv_cache_hit_estimate, tokens_generated, latency_ms, error_code, kernel-hints. Use JSONL at 1k/s sampling for high-volume routes.

Recommended capture command:
```
trace-proxy capture --router $ROUTE --write /tmp/captures/$ROUTE-2026-02-01.jsonl --sample-rate 0.01 --fields timestamp,request_id,session_id,model,route,seq_in,seq_out_cap,kv_hint,latency_ms,error
```

Normalization and derived signals:
- tokens_per_request = seq_in + median(seq_out_observed if available else seq_out_cap)
- burstiness = count(requests within 1s windows) distribution
- continuity_index = fraction(session_id consecutive requests share model/version)

Output artifact: workload-profile.json (canonical format used by perf-harness). Example snippet:
```
{
  "route": "search-completions",
  "time_window": "2026-02-01T08:00:00Z/2026-02-01T12:00:00Z",
  "seq_len_p50": "48",
  "seq_len_p95": "224",
  "tokens_p_request_avg": "132",
  "kv_affinity": "0.72",
  "burst_percentile_99": "34"
}
```

2) Benchmark matrix & experiment design
---------------------------------------
Design an experiment that spans: hardware classes, model variants (fp16, q4_k, q8_0), kernel configurations (continuous batching on/off, slot size, preemption policy), and traffic shapes (steady, microburst, session-affine).

Minimum matrix entries for a production acceptance test:
- Hardware: {H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB}
- Model variants: {fp16, q4_k, q8_0}
- Scheduler presets: {latency-tilt, throughput-tilt, balanced}
- Traffic shapes: {baseline-day, microburst-peak, long-seq-synth}

For each run collect: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization (SM%, mem%), kernel queue length, kernel dispatch time histogram, energy-per-token estimate.

Acceptance criteria (example):
- p99 <= declared SLO + 15% (safety buffer) on latency-tilt config for baseline-day shape.
- tokens/sec per GPU meets committed reserve for Dedicated customers within 10%.
- model-quality regression: automatic eval set must show BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity delta < defined threshold.

3) Scheduler & kernel evaluation checklist
-----------------------------------------
Primary knobs to sweep and why:
- batch_size_max: affects amortized kernel overhead and tail latency. Sweep 1, 4, 8, 16 for short sequences.
- batch_wait_ms: tradeoff between latency and throughput for bursty traffic.
- preemption_policy: eager | cooperative | disabled. Use cooperative on multi-tenant pools.
- slot_quota / tenant_credits: enforces fairness under contention.
- kernel_hint: prefer fused_attention | sharded_attention | memory_opt; used to surface specialized kernels.

Evaluator actions:
1. Run low-load baseline to establish kernel latency floor per kernel_hint.
2. Inject mixed-priority synthetic load to measure priority inversion and starvation risk.
3. Toggle preemption to gauge warm-start cost vs p99 improvement.
4. Measure KV-cache warmup curve: cold -> 30m -> 2h to estimate steady-state cost savings.

Suggested result table (example lines):
"Hardware | Kernel_hint | batch_size | p50 | p95 | p99 | tokens/s | SM% | Notes"
"H100 | fused_attention_v2 | 8 | 22ms | 48ms | 120ms | 4200 | 73% | Best for long seqs"

4) Profiling recipe (trace to remediation)
-----------------------------------------
Trigger: p99 regression or new kernel rollout.

Rapid triage steps (first 20 minutes):
1. Confirm scope: route(s) affected, time window, customer impact. Use kibana/route-dashboard.
2. Pull canonical workload-profile for the route. If production profile changed >10% on seq_len_p95 or burstiness, mark as traffic-shift.
3. Enable detailed trace-proxy sampling for the affected route (raise sample rate to 1%).
4. Correlate trace IDs with runtime kernel traces (kernel-trace tool) to determine slow kernels.
  - kernel-trace aggregate --start TS1 --end TS2 --group-by kernel_hint --metric mean_dispatch_ms,p95_dispatch_ms
5. If kernel dispatch time increased but SM% unchanged -> suspect kernel regression (new codepath or compilation change).
6. If SM% spiked and memory pressure rose -> suspect increased concurrency or larger batch sizing; check eviction logs.

Common remedial actions:
- Rollback kernel rollout via feature-flag: runtime-flag set kernel_selector=stable
- For memory pressure: reduce batch_size_max and enable eager-eviction for ephemeral caches
- For priority inversion: temporarily raise tenant_credits for affected route or enable emergency quota-exemption for critical traffic

5) Cost & capacity guidance (back-of-envelope models)
-----------------------------------------------------
Unit economics inputs:
- tokens_per_request (from fingerprint)
- tokens_per_second_per_GPU (measured in benchmark)
- cloud GPU $/hr (from procurement table)
- target utilization (70–80% for Dedicated pools)

Example calculation (string form):
"Provisioned GPUs = ceil(peak_tokens_per_sec / tokens_per_second_per_GPU / target_utilization)"

Quick example: average tokens/sec required = 500k -> tokens_per_gpu = 4k -> target_util 0.75 -> GPUs = ceil(500000 / 4000 / 0.75) = 167 GPUs

6) Canary and rollout matrix for scheduler/kernel changes
--------------------------------------------------------
Principles:
- Small fast canaries: 0.5–1% traffic for 30 minutes with full traces enabled.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%, validate p99/p95 and per-route cost after each step.
- Safety gates: automatic rollback if p99 increases >20% or tokens/sec drops >15% vs baseline.

Recommended telemetry to watch during canary:
- route-p99, route-error-rate, kernel-dispatch-p95, gpu-eviction-rate, kv-warmup-slope.

Canary checklist (playbook):
1. Start at 0.5% for 30m, inspect traces and run the profiling recipe.
2. If all checks pass, extend to 5% for 1h, run full benchmark matrix for that period.
3. If any safety gate trips, rollback to previous kernel_selector and escalate to runtime-oncall.

7) Known issues inventory (operational notes)
-------------------------------------------
- Large-LLM microbursts causing slot exhaustion: mitigate with per-route burst_alloc and smaller batch windows.
- KV-cache skew across shards: drains during scale-up cause increased cold hits; schedule staggered warms on scale events.
- GPU memory fragmentation after quantization rollouts: periodic compaction job recommended during maintenance windows.
- Kernel regression from clang update: always run the hidden-kernel-regression-probe-suite before rollout.

8) Runbook extracts (for Pager/Slack responders)
------------------------------------------------
Symptom: sudden p99 increase for route X
- Pager owner: runtime-oncall
- Initial actions (within 10m):
  1. Confirm impact (dashboard p99 spike > configured alert threshold).
  2. Identify whether spike correlates with deployments or traffic-shift: check deploy-log and trace-capture.
  3. If deployment correlates, flip kernel_selector to previous stable tag and monitor for 10m.
  4. If traffic-shift, apply emergency throttles or temporary scaling policy to Dedicated pool.
  5. Open incident ticket with kernel traces attached and assign to oncall-engineer.

Symptom: elevated GPU OOMs during rollout
- Steps:
  1. Suspend rollout.
  2. Reduce batch_size_max by 50% across affected pool.
  3. Kick maintenance compaction job: gpu-mem-compact --pool $POOL --max-run 2h
  4. If OOMs persist, escalate to infra-gpu team.

9) Release notes template for runtime changes
-------------------------------------------
Use this compact template for each runtime release (kernel/scheduler/runtime binary):
- Release tag: x.y.z
- Owners: runtime-team
- Summary: one-sentence summary of user-facing impact
- Benchmarks run: matrix summary (hardware, routes, model variants)
- Canary plan: percentages + safety gates
- Known limitations: e.g., issues with T4 under long sequences
- Rollback steps: clear commands and feature-flag names
- Relevant artifacts: links to workload-profile(s) and perf-harness logs

10) Operational ownership and links
--------------------------------
- Primary owners: runtime-team (oncall rotation), perf-engineering for benchmark harness, infra-gpu for hardware incidents.
- Related pages and artifacts:
  - perf-harness repo: //git.internal/redwood/perf-harness
  - trace-proxy runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-trace-correlator-and-event-reconciliation-playbook-2025
  - canonical workload storage: s3://redwood-perf/workloads/

Appendices
----------
A. Example scheduler policy (YAML)
```
policy_name: latency-tilt-small-batches
batching:
  max_batch_size: 8
  batch_wait_ms: 6
preemption:
  policy: cooperative
  preempt_check_interval_ms: 50
quota:
  tenant_credit_mode: burstable
  default_quota_tokens_per_minute: 60000
kernel_hints:
  preferred: [fused_attention_v2, sharded_attention]
```

B. Quick commands (profiling)
- Pull kernel traces for window:
```
kernel-trace aggregate --route search-completions --start 2026-02-01T08:00:00Z --end 2026-02-01T09:00:00Z --out /tmp/kt.json
```
- Run synthetic microburst generator:
```
perf-harness loadgen --profile workload-profile.json --shape microburst --duration 15m --out /tmp/run-01
```
